Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette: Elias Vance was forty-five when the hurricane-force winds and rising water collapsed the field hospital where he served as a military medic. He remembered the exact moment the canvas walls tore open, not as a single picture, but as a suffocating rush of debris, the deafening roar of water, and the frantic, failing triage of men pinned under twisted support beams. For weeks afterward, the silence of his suburban home felt wrong. Even when he knew he was safe, he could not relax, his muscles permanently coiled as if another collapse were imminent. The environment of his daily life had shifted from a place of service to a landscape of potential failure, and he began to treat every routine moment like a fragile perimeter. His body never stopped scanning the aisles of the military medical supply depot where he continued to work. He stood superalert and watchful, his eyes darting to the ceiling whenever a shelving unit groaned or a forklift backfired. He became intolerant of unexpected or loud sounds, flinching violently when a heavy crate dropped on the concrete floor or when a pressure valve hissed during inspection. Over months, this relentless state of being on guard slowly eroded the architecture of his former life. Because his nervous system refused to accept that the storm had passed, his shattered beliefs about how the world works took root. He began to see his deployments not as tragedies to be processed, but as proof that the fundamental rules of safety had been completely destroyed, leaving him with a profound sense of lost meaning. The memories did not arrive as coherent stories. When the event returned, Elias found he could not put the memories of the event in the right order, the images jumping between collapsed stretchers, screaming patients, and the dark water rising past his boots. He would sit at his kitchen table until the overwhelm on recall became too much, feeling so flooded by emotion that he had to stop and leave the room. Yet, each time the memories intruded, they actively dismantled his sense of self. The terror on recall, stripped of any protective context, fed directly into his negative appraisals. He would look in the mirror and feel like he didn't know himself anymore, certain that the man who had once cared for others was now just a hollow shell watching his own life slip away. The way he viewed his present reality dictated how the past continued to invade his days. His lost meaning and identity loss acted like a dark lens, warping how he accessed the event. Because he had come to believe that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore and that his own moral compass had been obliterated, the trauma memories surfaced with intensified ferocity. His shattered beliefs stripped the memories of any therapeutic distance, pulling the terror on recall forward with violent urgency. Every time he tried to ground himself, the conviction that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed ensured that the memories returned not as recollections, but as immediate, inescapable threats. He had stopped entering the depot’s loading bay, unable to face the rolling crates of oxygen tanks or the sharp whine of pneumatic doors. His wife had died two years prior to the storm, and his isolation had deepened into a rigid routine of staying indoors, curtains drawn, listening to the rhythmic click of a ceiling fan just to mask the silence. The consequences were concrete: he could no longer sit through veteran gatherings, and the constant inability to relax meant he slept in twenty-minute increments. Finally, after a panic attack while watching a storm tracker on television, he scheduled an appointment with a trauma specialist. He was most afraid of what the therapist might ask him to remember, yet he hoped, against all his new convictions, that someone might help him untangle the loop keeping him trapped.
